body:
The first move is to stop trying to settle what the old agreement meant. You likely had a real agreement, but it was underspecified: who, what standard, by when, and what happens if schedules change. Arguing about the past will mostly produce defensiveness. Reframe it as: we keep having the same fight because our system relies on memory and goodwill. Can we spend thirty minutes designing a minimum system, then test it?

Propose concrete definitions. For each recurring chore, write down owner or rotation, exact task, standard, frequency, deadline, and swap rule. Example: kitchen reset means dishes washed, counters cleared and wiped, trash taken out if full; done by 10 p.m. on your assigned day. If you cannot do it, you must ask for a swap at least 24 hours before, or by a set time, not just skip. Put it somewhere shared and visible: whiteboard, note, shared doc. Assign ownership rather than vague shared responsibility where possible.

Build in schedule change. Use a monthly rotation or a bidding system: people pick chores they prefer, then rotate the rest. Review at a short weekly or fortnightly check-in, ten minutes, standing up. Keep a running list of exceptions. If one person avoids the conversation, do not make the group meeting the only channel. Ask them privately what makes it hard: timing, conflict, feeling ganged up on, not knowing what is expected. Offer async updates or a one-on-one first. If they still will not engage, the issue is no longer only chores; it is whether the household can make decisions together.

Aim for fair, not identical. Fairness can mean equal time, equal unpleasantness, or traded preferences. If someone has a brutal work week, they can trade rather than silently fail. Consider a paid cleaner for common areas if affordable; that can be cheaper than resentment. Keep your own boundaries: clean your own mess, use your own dishes if needed, and do not silently absorb everything. If the system fails after a fair trial, decide what you will do, including whether this flat still works.
commitments:
Taking this up would involve proposing a reset conversation framed as fixing the process rather than relitigating past chores; drafting a one-page charter with concrete definitions, owners, deadlines, and swap rules; running it as a two-to-four week trial; and holding a short review. It depends on all three being willing to try, or at least on the two willing flatmates not using it as a weapon against the third. If the avoiding friend will not join a group meeting, I would first try a private low-pressure conversation and an async written option; if that fails, the proposal narrows to what you and the other willing flatmate can do and to deciding whether to stay.

The claim that written specificity reduces disputes is a prediction, not a guarantee. It should be judged by whether arguments become less frequent and more concrete, not by whether everyone suddenly likes chores. I would criticize this approach as potentially bureaucratic, and as possibly over-focusing on fairness accounting while missing burnout, stress, or mental health. Unresolved: what to do if standards differ irreconcilably, whether a paid cleaner is acceptable, and how long to persist before treating the living arrangement itself as the problem. I would not treat the charter as a truth certificate or a permanent constitution; I would revise or drop it if it increases resentment or if the flatmates will not honestly use it.
